topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Compute Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school or undergraduate students with basic physics and geometry knowledge

outline.topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Compute Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school or undergraduate students with basic physics and geometry knowledge

sections.title: The Setup: The Elastic Collision Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce a 1D physics environment with two blocks on a frictionless surface: a small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M). The small block moves toward the large one, which is at rest. Both bounce elastically against each other and a wall behind the small block.
sections.example: A toy car (mass m) zipping toward a massive freight train (mass M) while a solid wall is behind the toy car.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conservation of Momentum and Energy
sections.content: Briefly explain that in elastic collisions, both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved. Use vector arrows to show velocity reversals upon impact with the wall and the exchange of momentum during block-to-block collisions.
sections.example: Visualizing velocity vectors: Before (v1, 0) vs After (v1', v2') using simple billiard ball diagrams.

sections.title: The Scaling Phenomenon: The Role of Mass Ratio
sections.content: State the counter-intuitive observation: if mass M = 100^n * m, the total number of collisions in the system will yield the first n+1 digits of Pi (e.g., if M = 100m, collisions = 31). Explain that as the mass ratio increases, the physics mimics the reflection of a light ray in a circular geometry.
sections.example: A table showing Mass Ratio 1:1, 1:100, 1:10000 leading to collision counts 3, 31, 314.

sections.title: Geometric Visualization: Unfolding the Collisions
sections.content: Show that the motion of the two blocks can be mapped onto a 2D plane as a billiard ball reflecting inside a wedge with an angle of theta = arcsin(sqrt(m/M)). As the blocks bounce, the path traces the perimeter of a circle or arc, effectively calculating Pi.
sections.example: An animation transforming 1D motion on a line into a 2D 'unfolded' trajectory hitting the boundaries of a circular sector.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Mathematical Equivalence
sections.content: Summarize that Pi appears not because of 'circular' motion, but because the phase space of the collision is topologically equivalent to the geometry of a circle. Final thought: Physics and pure math are often different languages describing the same underlying structure.
sections.example: Final slide: A 'Code-Breaking' graphic where physical blocks 'solve' the digits of Pi, revealing the hidden order in the chaos.
